title: Big data in real applications
summary: This chapter applies the course's stack (Kafka, Spark, HDFS, Hive, Grafana) to three domains: social media graphs, time series forecasting and healthcare data. A flu surveillance case study shows what big data signals can and cannot replace.

topics.title: Social media as a graph: communities, influence, Twitter's shape
facts: Four data dimensions of social media: graph-structured, temporal, text (NLP), multimedia.
The graph (who follows or retweets whom) is the main object of analysis, not the single post.
Community: nodes more densely linked to each other than to the rest of the graph. Found with Louvain (Blondel 2008), O(n log n).
Modularity: fraction of edges inside communities minus the fraction expected by chance. Louvain maximises it.
Influence maximisation: choose k seed users so a message spreads furthest. NP-hard; Kempe's greedy method guarantees (1 − 1/e) ≈ 63% of optimal.
Kwak 2010: 41.7M users, 1.47B directed edges, 22.1% mutual follows, power law α ≈ 2.276, average shortest path 4.12 hops, 85% of trends are news.
Kwak 2010 impact: seeding a campaign at high-PageRank users gives measurably different spread from seeding at high-follower users, so follower count is not the same as influence.
mechanism: Louvain start: every node is its own community
Move each node into the neighbour community that gives the biggest modularity gain
Collapse each community into one super-node (edges between communities become weighted edges)
Repeat the move and collapse steps on the smaller graph
Stop when no move raises modularity (gain is zero)
why: Louvain is greedy and local, so it scales to billion-node graphs in Spark GraphX.
Modularity compares against chance, so a big group is not called a community just for being big.
Exact influence maximisation is NP-hard; greedy gives a proven 63% floor in reasonable time.
Twitter is sparse: 1.47B edges among 41.7M users is about 35 follows each, a tiny share of possible links.
Low reciprocity and fast news trends make Twitter a news medium, which is why health agencies watch it.

traps: PageRank measures importance, not community membership; K-Means clusters vectors, not graph links.
The hop estimate is an upper bound: it counts shared followers again (clustering, overlapping neighbourhoods).
Kempe's result: the problem is NP-hard, the greedy answer is approximate (63%), not exact.

answers.1: Community detection finds groups of nodes more densely linked to each other than to the rest of the graph, usually with the Louvain algorithm.
answers.3: Louvain starts with each node alone, greedily merges nodes to raise modularity (edges inside groups minus the chance level), collapses groups into super-nodes and repeats until modularity stops rising. It runs in O(n log n), so it handles billion-node graphs. Example: finding a bot network that retweets only itself.
answers.5: Social media data is a graph: users are nodes, follows and retweets are edges. Community detection (Louvain) finds densely linked groups: start with each node alone, merge to raise modularity, collapse into super-nodes, repeat until no gain. Influence maximisation picks k seeds for widest spread; it is NP-hard, so Kempe's greedy method is used with a (1 − 1/e) ≈ 63% guarantee. Example: Kwak 2010 found Twitter has 41.7M users, 22.1% mutual follows and 4.12 average hops, so it acts as a news medium. With out-degree 45, a tweet reaches at most 93,195 users in 3 hops. Limitation: that estimate ignores overlapping followers, so it is too high.

questions.q: Which algorithm is designed to find communities by maximising modularity?
questions.a: Louvain greedily merges nodes to raise modularity; PageRank ranks node importance.

questions.q: Kempe et al. showed influence maximisation is ______, and the greedy method reaches at least ______ of the optimal spread.
questions.a: NP-hard; (1 − 1/e) ≈ 63%

questions.q: Define modularity and list the four data dimensions of social media.
questions.a: Modularity: fraction of edges inside communities minus the fraction expected by chance. Dimensions: graph-structured, temporal, text (NLP), multimedia.

questions.q: Describe the steps of the Louvain algorithm.
questions.a:
1. Each node is its own community.
  2. Move each node to the neighbour community with the largest modularity gain.
  3. Collapse communities into super-nodes.
  4. Repeat.
  5. Stop when the gain is zero.

questions.q: Why is Twitter called a news medium rather than a social network?
questions.a: Only 22.1% of follows are mutual, follower counts follow a power law with a few huge hubs, and 85% of trending topics are headline news (Kwak 2010).

questions.q: Distinguish community detection from PageRank.
questions.a: Community detection assigns each node to a densely linked group (Louvain, modularity). PageRank gives each node an importance score. One answers 'which group', the other 'how important'.

questions.q:
A watchdog studies 2 million Bangla Facebook accounts that share election posts.
i) It wants groups that mostly share among themselves. Which method? ii) It wants 20 accounts to seed a fact-check. Which problem is this? iii) What guarantee does the greedy answer carry? iv) Each account shares to 40 others. Upper bound on reach in 2 hops?
questions.a: i) Community detection with Louvain. ii) Influence maximisation. iii) At least (1 − 1/e) ≈ 63% of the optimal spread. iv) 40 + 1,600 = 1,640 users.

questions.q: Hop 2 of a cascade reached 2,025 users and the average out-degree is 45. How many new users at hop 3?
A tweet starts at one account. Average out-degree 30. Estimate users reached within 3 hops, and say why the real number is lower.
questions.a: 30 + 30² + 30³ = 30 + 900 + 27,000 = 27,930. Lower in reality because followers overlap (clustering), so the same people are counted again, and most people do not retweet.

questions.q: Explain how social media graphs are analysed, covering community detection, influence maximisation and the structure Kwak et al. found on Twitter.
questions.a: Use the 5-mark answer: graph model, Louvain steps and modularity, influence maximisation with the 63% greedy guarantee, Kwak's 22.1% reciprocity, power law and 4.12 hops, then the 3-hop reach of 93,195 as an upper bound.

diagram.caption: Communities are dense inside and sparsely linked between, which is what Louvain's modularity rewards; a hub bridges them.

topics.title: Sentiment (VADER), trend detection and ethics
facts: VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary for Sentiment Reasoning (Hutto & Gilbert 2014), lexicon-and-rule based, tuned for social media text.
VADER handles capitalisation, punctuation (!!!), degree words (very, kind of), negation (not good) and emojis.
Compound score in [−1, +1]: > 0.05 positive, < −0.05 negative, otherwise neutral.
Trend detection: Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) on character n-grams finds phrases whose frequency jumps against their own baseline.
Slide example: 10 per hour to 10,000 per hour is trending regardless of absolute volume. #QurbaniEid: 1,200× spike in 6 hours, 92% positive.
Ethical risks: suppressing dissent, microtargeting vulnerable users. Safeguards: transparency and purpose limitation.
mechanism: Read tweets into a Spark DataFrame (from Kafka)
Apply VADER to each tweet with a UDF to get a compound score
Label each tweet positive, neutral or negative with the 0.05 cut-offs
Aggregate scores by time window and topic
In parallel, count each phrase per hour and divide by its historical baseline to flag spikes
Push the aggregates to the Grafana streaming dashboard (Week 9)
why: Rules and a lexicon need no labelled training data, so VADER works out of the box on short, noisy posts.
Comparing to a phrase's own baseline catches a small topic that suddenly explodes, which raw counts would miss.
Sentiment on a spike tells organic celebration from coordinated activity (#QurbaniEid was 92% positive).
Limitation: an English lexicon misreads Bangla, slang and sarcasm, so it needs a Bangla lexicon added.
The same scores that track public mood can flag critics, so purpose limits are needed.

calculation.example:
P1 slide 12: a phrase goes from 10/hour to 10,000/hour.

Spike ratio = current / baseline = 10,000 / 10 = 1,000×, so it is trending.

VADER on three posts: 0.62, 0.03, −0.40 → positive, neutral, negative.
steps: Given a compound of 0.03 -> between −0.05 and 0.05, neutral
variants: #QurbaniEid spike 1,200× on a baseline of 50 posts/hour: peak = 50 × 1,200 = 60,000 posts/hour.
Compound exactly 0.05: not greater than 0.05, so neutral by the slide's rule (VADER's own docs, using ≥ 0.05, would call it positive). −0.06: negative.

traps: The slide's cut-offs are strict (> 0.05, < −0.05), so 0.05 itself is neutral by the slide. VADER's own documentation uses ≥ 0.05 and ≤ −0.05, so if a boundary value is asked, state the slide's rule you are using.
Trending depends on the ratio to baseline, not on absolute volume.
VADER is rule-based, not a deep-learning classifier.
LSH here is for detecting trends, not for sentiment.

answers.1: VADER is a lexicon-and-rule-based sentiment analyser for social media that outputs a compound score in [−1, +1].
answers.3: VADER scores each post using a word list plus rules for capitals, punctuation, degree words, negation and emojis. Compound above 0.05 is positive and below −0.05 is negative. Example: 'NOT good!!!' scores more negative than 'not good'.
answers.5: Sentiment analysis scores text as positive, neutral or negative. VADER uses a lexicon and rules (capitals, !!!, very, not, emojis) and gives a compound score in [−1, +1] with ±0.05 cut-offs. In Spark it runs as a UDF, then scores are aggregated by window and topic and sent to Grafana. Trend detection uses LSH on character n-grams and flags a phrase whose rate jumps against its baseline: 10 to 10,000 per hour is 1,000×. Example: #QurbaniEid spiked 1,200× and was 92% positive, so it was organic. Limitation: it can be used to flag critics, so transparency and purpose limitation are required.

questions.q: A VADER compound score of −0.03 is classed as:
questions.a: Negative needs a score below −0.05; −0.03 is in the neutral band.

questions.q: Twitter's trending algorithm uses ______ on character n-grams to detect spikes relative to a phrase's ______.
questions.a: Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH); historical baseline

questions.q: Define VADER and list five text features it handles.
questions.a: A lexicon-and-rule-based sentiment analyser tuned for social media. Handles capitalisation, punctuation, degree modifiers, negation, emojis.

questions.q: Describe a Spark pipeline for streaming tweet sentiment.
questions.a:
1. Read tweets from Kafka into a DataFrame.
  2. Apply VADER as a UDF.
  3. Label with ±0.05 cut-offs.
  4. Aggregate by time window and topic.
  5. Push to Grafana.

questions.q: Why does trend detection compare to a phrase's baseline instead of using raw counts?
questions.a: Big topics are always high. A ratio catches a small phrase that suddenly explodes (10 to 10,000 per hour) regardless of absolute volume.

questions.q: Distinguish sentiment analysis from trend detection.
questions.a: Sentiment analysis asks how people feel in each post (VADER score). Trend detection asks which phrase is suddenly more frequent than usual (spike ratio). They combine: score the posts inside a spike.

questions.q:
During a flood, a hashtag about relief goods rises from 40 to 8,000 posts an hour. Analysts run VADER on it.
i) What is the spike ratio? ii) Is it trending? iii) A post scores 0.04. Class? iv) Name one ethical risk if the government uses this to find critics.
questions.a: i) 8,000 / 40 = 200×. ii) Yes, it jumped far above its baseline. iii) Neutral (between −0.05 and 0.05). iv) Suppressing dissent.

questions.q: A phrase's baseline is 50 posts/hour and the spike is 1,200×. Peak rate?
questions.a: 50 × 1,200 = 60,000 posts/hour.

questions.q: Baseline 20/hour, current 6,000/hour. Three posts in the spike score 0.70, −0.02, −0.30. Give the ratio and the three classes.
questions.a: 6,000 / 20 = 300×. 0.70 positive; −0.02 neutral; −0.30 negative.

questions.q: Explain sentiment analysis and trend detection on social media, with one Bangladesh example and the ethical risks.
questions.a: Use the 5-mark answer: VADER features and cut-offs, the Spark UDF pipeline, LSH spike ratio, #QurbaniEid (1,200×, 92% positive), then suppressing dissent and microtargeting, with transparency and purpose limitation.

diagram.caption: VADER splits the compound score at ±0.05, and trend detection divides a phrase's current rate by its own baseline.

topics.title: Time series, ARIMA and Prophet at scale
facts: Time series properties: order matters, autocorrelation, seasonality, trend, non-stationarity (mean and variance change over time).
ARIMA(p, d, q): AR uses past p values, I differences d times for stationarity, MA uses past q forecast errors.
Prophet (Taylor & Letham 2018): y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t): trend, seasonality, holidays, noise.
g(t) is piecewise linear or logistic with automatic changepoints; s(t) is a Fourier series, P = 365.25 (yearly) or 7 (weekly).
changepoint_prior_scale sets trend flexibility: 0.05 default (stiff), 0.5 flexible. Default uncertainty band is 80%.
Spark: groupBy(sku_id).applyInPandas fits 5,000 Prophet models in parallel: 8 hours to about 12 minutes on 20 executors (40×).
mechanism: Load all SKU series into one Spark DataFrame, one row per day per SKU
Group by sku_id, so each group is one independent series
applyInPandas sends each group to one task as a Pandas DataFrame
Inside the function, fit Prophet on columns ds and y and predict 90 days ahead
All 5,000 models fit in parallel across the cluster
Write forecasts to Hive/S3 as Parquet and serve them to the dashboard
why: Shuffling a time series destroys trend and seasonality, so standard i.i.d. regression is invalid.
ARIMA needs stationarity, struggles with several seasonal cycles and needs an expert to pick p, d, q, so it cannot be hand-fitted for 10,000 series.
Prophet's parts are readable, so analysts (not statisticians) can add holidays and adjust trend flexibility.
A sparse prior on the slope changes δ keeps most changepoints near zero, which avoids overfitting.
Each series is fitted independently, so the job is embarrassingly parallel in Spark.

steps: Given 480 min sequential and 12 min parallel -> speedup = 480 / 12 = 40×
Given 8 h = 28,800 s and 5,000 models -> 5.76 s per model
Given 5,000 models and 20 executors -> 250 models per executor

Changepoint at t = 10: k = 0.5, m = 1, δ = 0.3, γ = −3. g(10) = 6 both sides, g(20) = 0.8 × 20 + 1 − 3 = 14.

Lecturer's textbook (ch 10): 6,000 towers at 2 s per Prophet fit. Sequential 12,000 s; one 8-core machine 12,000 / 8 = 1,500 s = 25 min; 20 executors × 8 cores = 160 slots: 6,000 / 160 = 37.5, so 38 rounds × 2 s = 76 s.

traps: A sudden wave is a trend changepoint, not seasonality; h(t) only covers dates you list in advance.
Weekly seasonality on weekly data learns nothing: every point is the same weekday.
Prophet's default interval is 80%; set interval_width=0.95 for 95%.
ARIMA's d is the number of differences, not the number of seasons.

answers.1: Prophet is a time series forecasting model that splits a series into trend, seasonality, holidays and noise: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t).
answers.3: ARIMA(p, d, q) predicts from past values and past errors after differencing to stationarity, and needs an expert to tune it. Prophet adds a changepoint trend, Fourier seasonality and a holiday term, and tunes itself, so it scales to thousands of series. Example: 5,000 SKU forecasts drop from 8 hours to 12 minutes with applyInPandas.
answers.5: Time series data is ordered and autocorrelated, with trend and seasonality. ARIMA(p, d, q) needs stationary input and expert tuning, so it fails at 10,000 series. Prophet fits y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t): piecewise trend with automatic changepoints, Fourier seasonality (P = 365.25, 7), user-listed holidays. At scale: group by sku_id, applyInPandas fits one Prophet per group in parallel, write Parquet to Hive/S3. Example: 5,000 SKUs, 8 h to 12 min on 20 executors, 40×. Limitation: with the default changepoint_prior_scale of 0.05 the trend is stiff and can miss a sudden break.

questions.q: In Prophet, which component should capture a sudden, unplanned shift in the level of a series?
questions.a: A break is a trend changepoint; h(t) covers only listed dates and s(t) only repeating cycles.

questions.q: In ARIMA(p, d, q), d is the number of times the series is ______ to make it ______.
questions.a: differenced; stationary

questions.q: Define stationarity and list the four terms of the Prophet model.
questions.a: A stationary series has constant mean and variance over time. Terms: trend g(t), seasonality s(t), holidays h(t), noise ε(t).

questions.q: Describe how Spark fits 5,000 Prophet models in parallel.
questions.a:
1. One DataFrame, a row per day per SKU.
  2. groupBy sku_id.
  3. applyInPandas sends each group to a task.
  4. Prophet fits and forecasts inside the Pandas UDF.
  5. All fit in parallel.
  6. Write Parquet to Hive/S3, serve to dashboard.

questions.q: Why can ARIMA not be used for 10,000 series at big data scale?
questions.a: Each series needs stationarity checks and an expert to choose p, d, q. That manual tuning cannot be repeated 10,000 times.

questions.q: Distinguish ARIMA from Prophet.
questions.a: ARIMA: past values and errors, stationary input, expert tuning, weak on multiple seasonality, no holidays. Prophet: additive trend + Fourier seasonality + holidays, automatic, readable, parallel in Spark.

questions.q:
A pharmacy chain forecasts daily sales for 5,000 SKUs. It takes 8 hours on one server.
i) Which model fits Eid effects? ii) Which Spark call parallelises it? iii) Speedup if it now takes 12 minutes? iv) Name the slowest step.
questions.a: i) Prophet with a holiday list. ii) groupBy('sku_id').applyInPandas. iii) 480 / 12 = 40×. iv) Model fitting (Prophet via Stan).

questions.q: Fitting 5,000 models sequentially takes 8 hours. Time per model in seconds?
10,000 SKUs, 5.76 s per model, 40 models fit at once. Sequential time, parallel time and speedup?
Explain time series forecasting at big data scale: what makes time series special, ARIMA's limits, Prophet's model and how Spark scales it.
questions.a: Use the 5-mark answer: five properties, ARIMA(p, d, q) and its three limits, Prophet's four terms with changepoints and Fourier, the applyInPandas steps, the 40× example, the stiff-trend limitation.

topics.title: Anomaly detection: STL and Isolation Forest
facts: Anomaly: a data point that does not conform to the expected pattern (outlier, change point or contextual deviation).
STL: Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS. Splits a series into trend, seasonal and residual.
STL rule: flag a point if |residual| > k × IQR of the residuals (IQR = Q3 − Q1).
Isolation Forest: an ensemble of random trees; an anomaly needs fewer splits to isolate, so its path is shorter.
Isolation Forest assumes no data distribution and scales to millions of points in Spark MLlib.
Slide example: bKash agent jumps from 10 to 10,000 transactions per hour, flagged as possible money laundering.
mechanism: STL: decompose the series into trend, seasonal and residual parts
Compute Q1, Q3 and IQR of the residuals
Flag points with |residual| above k × IQR
Isolation Forest: build many random trees, each splitting on a random feature at a random value
Measure how many splits each point needs to be isolated
Short average path length means anomaly
why: Removing trend and seasonality first stops a normal winter peak from being flagged.
IQR ignores extreme values, so one huge spike does not hide itself by inflating the threshold.
STL is interpretable and works well when seasonality is regular.
Isolation Forest needs no distribution assumption and handles many features, such as per-agent volumes.
Odd points sit alone, so random cuts separate them quickly.

Isolation Forest

scenarios.cue: an agent's hourly transactions jump from 10 to 10,000
flag days whose value is far off after removing the weekly and yearly cycle
a wearable streams heart rate per second and a sudden drop must raise an alert
scenarios.answer: streaming anomaly detection on time series

calculation.example:
Residuals: 0.2, −0.1, 0.3, −0.4, 0.1, 5.0, −0.2, 0.0; k = 3.

  1. Sorted: −0.4, −0.2, −0.1, 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 5.0
  2. Q1 = −0.125, Q3 = 0.225 (inclusive interpolation)
  3. IQR = 0.35; threshold = 3 × 0.35 = 1.05
  4. Only |5.0| > 1.05: the 6th point is the anomaly
steps: Given the sorted list -> Q1 = −0.125, Q3 = 0.225
Given threshold 1.05 -> compare each |residual|; only 5.0 exceeds it
variants: Same data, k = 1.5: threshold 0.525; largest normal |−0.4| = 0.4, so still only 5.0 is flagged.
IQR = 2 and k = 3: threshold 6, a residual of −7 is flagged (absolute value).

traps: Use the absolute value of the residual: big negative residuals are anomalies too.
The threshold uses the IQR of residuals, not of the raw series.
In Isolation Forest, anomalies have shorter paths, not longer.

answers.1: An anomaly is a data point that does not conform to the expected pattern of the series.
answers.3: STL splits the series into trend, seasonal and residual, then flags points whose |residual| exceeds k × IQR. Isolation Forest builds random trees and flags points that need few splits to isolate. Example: a bKash agent jumping from 10 to 10,000 transactions an hour.
answers.5: An anomaly does not fit the expected pattern. STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS): decompose into trend, seasonal, residual; compute the residuals' IQR; flag |residual| > k × IQR. Example: residuals with IQR 0.35 and k = 3 give threshold 1.05, so a residual of 5.0 is flagged. Isolation Forest: random trees cut the feature space; anomalies are isolated in fewer splits. It assumes no distribution and scales in Spark MLlib, as in bKash's per-agent monitoring. Limitation: STL needs regular seasonality, and k is a choice the slide leaves open.

questions.q: In an Isolation Forest, an anomaly is a point that:
options: Needs fewer random splits to isolate
Needs more random splits to isolate
Lies closest to a cluster centroid
questions.a: Odd points sit alone, so random cuts reach them quickly: shorter path length.

questions.q: STL flags a point when its absolute ______ exceeds k × ______.
questions.a: residual; IQR of the residuals

questions.q: Define anomaly and list the three parts STL produces.
questions.a: A point that does not conform to the expected pattern. Trend, seasonal, residual.

questions.q: Describe STL anomaly detection.
questions.a:
1. Decompose into trend, seasonal, residual.
  2. Find Q1, Q3, IQR of residuals.
  3. Threshold = k × IQR.
  4. Flag |residual| above it.

questions.q: Why remove trend and seasonality before looking for anomalies?
questions.a: Otherwise a normal seasonal peak (every winter) looks extreme. The residual shows only what the pattern cannot explain.

questions.q: Distinguish STL from Isolation Forest.
questions.a: STL: one seasonal series, flags large residuals, interpretable. Isolation Forest: random trees on many features, flags short-path points, no distribution assumption, scales in Spark MLlib.

questions.q:
bKash monitors hourly transactions per agent. One agent goes from 10 to 10,000.
i) Which method does the slide use? ii) Why is this point easy for it? iii) What is the spike ratio? iv) What might it indicate?
questions.a: i) Isolation Forest. ii) It sits far from all others, so few splits isolate it. iii) 10,000 / 10 = 1,000×. iv) Possible money laundering.

questions.q: Residual IQR is 0.35 and k = 3. What is the threshold?
Residuals 0.2, −0.1, 0.3, −0.4, 0.1, 5.0, −0.2, 0.0. With k = 1.5, which points are anomalies?
questions.a: Q1 = −0.125, Q3 = 0.225, IQR = 0.35, threshold 0.525. Only 5.0 is flagged.

questions.q: Explain two methods for anomaly detection in big time series data, with an example.
questions.a: Use the 5-mark answer: definition, STL steps and the worked threshold, Isolation Forest idea and bKash example, limitations.

topics.title: Healthcare big data, privacy and AlphaFold
facts: Four modalities: EHR (ICD-10, notes, FHIR), genomics (≈200 GB per genome; 10,000 patients = 2 PB), wearables (per-second), imaging (DICOM, 200 MB-2 GB, unstructured).
EHR ML beats physician rules: ICU mortality (random forest, AUROC > 0.90), 30-day readmission (20% fewer), sepsis 6 hours earlier. Needs 1M+ records.
HIPAA (USA): de-identify 18 PHI identifiers before research; consent. GDPR (EU): minimisation, purpose limitation, right to erasure.
PDPA Bangladesh: under development, GDPR-based; NID-linked records need explicit consent.
Protection: safe harbour, expert determination, differential privacy (calibrated noise on aggregates), federated learning (train at each hospital, data stays).
AlphaFold 2: 3D protein structure from amino-acid sequence; 170,000 PDB structures, MSAs over 250M UniProt sequences; 200M structures released 2022; 2024 Nobel.
mechanism: EHR arrives as FHIR resources, genomics as Parquet, wearables through Kafka, images as DICOM
All land in a health data lake on HDFS/S3 with a Hive Metastore catalogue
De-identify records before research use (remove the 18 identifiers)
Train clinical ML models: readmission, mortality, imaging CNNs, variant calling
Where records cannot move, train with federated learning; publish aggregates with differential privacy

topics.title: Syndromic surveillance and the Google Flu Trends lesson
facts: Physician-reported cases reach CDC 1 to 2 weeks after symptoms (ILINet: >3,000 sentinel physicians, weekly).
Syndromic surveillance uses pre-diagnosis signals: posts peak 7 to 10 days before ER visits; pharmacy antipyretic sales spike 3 to 5 days before confirmation.
Other signals: ER chief complaints via NLP; search volume (1-week lead).
BioSense: near real-time data from 3,500+ emergency departments; syndromes extracted automatically.
Google Flu Trends: r² = 0.97 on 2003-2008 data, then over-predicted flu by 2× in 2012-2013 and was discontinued.

Lazer et al. (2014), three causes of the GFT failure (P2 s14): big data hubris (r² = 0.97 on 5 training years did not generalise); algorithm confounding (Google's autocomplete changes shifted the search features); media amplification (flu news drove searches while incidence was low).
Post-GFT: BioSense ED visits as the main signal, Prophet for seasonality and season-start changepoints, Twitter as a covariate, ensembles (FluSight).
Twitter adds lead time, not accuracy: its signal arrives about 2 weeks before ILINet but with about 30% higher error (latency vs precision).
mechanism: Sources: Twitter (NLP), pharmacy sales, ER chief complaints, search trends
All publish events to a Kafka event bus
Spark Streaming runs NLP and aggregates counts per region and time window
An alert engine fires when a count breaches its threshold
A Grafana dashboard shows the signals to health officers
Officers confirm against clinical reporting before acting
why: Outbreaks grow exponentially, so a 1 to 2 week reporting lag is costly.
Proxy data measures behaviour (health anxiety, media coverage), not incidence, so it drifts.
GFT failed partly because Google's own autocomplete changes, opaque to CDC, shifted the features.
Prophet's g + s + h parts let epidemiologists inspect each piece, unlike black-box models.
High in-sample r² does not guarantee out-of-sample accuracy when behaviour changes.

pool.q: Time series data is order-sensitive: randomly shuffling the records in a time series changes the analysis result.

AnalysisWhat it doesEthical risk at scale

pool.q: What is the difference between ARIMA and Facebook Prophet for time series forecasting? Under what conditions would you prefer Prophet over ARIMA? When might ARIMA still be the better choice?
pool.a:
ARIMA(p, d, q) predicts from past p values and past q errors after differencing d times to make the series stationary. Prophet adds up trend with changepoints, Fourier seasonality and a holiday term: y = g + s + h + ε.

Prefer Prophet when the series has several seasonalities, holiday effects (Eid, Puja), trend shifts, missing data or outliers, or when thousands of series must be fitted automatically (5,000 SKUs in 12 minutes with applyInPandas).

ARIMA is still better for a short, stationary series with no strong seasonality and little data, where an expert can tune one important series closely.

(Name specific NLP features and pharmacy signal metrics) (c) What model would you use, and how would you validate it against ground-truth CDC/DGHS surveillance data? (d) What are the ethical risks of this system? How would you mitigate them?
pool.a:
Design: sources → Kafka → Spark Streaming → alert engine + Grafana (the CDC pattern).

PartSocial postsPharmacy sales
(a) IngestREST APIs (X API v2, Facebook Pages), keyword filter in Bangla and English, producer writes to Kafka topic social_rawSqoop for nightly bulk import from the chains' databases; Flume ships POS logs to Kafka topic pharmacy_sales
(b) FeaturesDaily flu-keyword post count per district; share of symptom terms (fever, cough, 'jor'); first-person illness flag; VADER/Bangla sentiment; ratio to 4-week baselineDaily paracetamol and cough-syrup units per district; week-on-week % change; z-score vs same week last year

(c) Model: Prophet per district on DGHS weekly ILI counts, yearly seasonality, Eid holidays, social and pharmacy features as extra regressors; run districts in parallel with applyInPandas. Validate with a rolling backtest against DGHS counts: error (MAE), lead time, hit rate, false alarms, and test on an unseen season (GFT had r² = 0.97 in-sample and still failed).

(d) Ethics: privacy (keep district counts only, drop user IDs, add differential-privacy noise); panic from false alarms (an officer confirms before any announcement); bias against rural and older people who post less (weight with pharmacy and DGHS data); misuse for watching individuals (purpose limitation, access logs, PDPA consent).

pool.q: Retail Demand Forecasting Pipeline: A large Bangladeshi supermarket chain needs 90-day demand forecasts for 5,000 store–product SKU combinations. Design the end-to-end big data pipeline: (a) data ingestion from POS systems; (b) storage and partitioning strategy in HDFS/S3; (c) forecasting model choice (ARIMA vs. Prophet vs. LSTM) and justification; (d) how you parallelise model fitting across 5,000 SKUs using Spark; (e) how forecasts are served to the inventory management dashboard. Identify the primary bottleneck in your pipeline.
pool.a:
StageDesign
(a) IngestTills send sale events to Kafka topic pos_sales; Sqoop bulk-loads history; Spark aggregates to (sku_id, date, units)
(b) StorageRaw Parquet on HDFS/S3 partitioned by date; daily aggregate Hive table partitioned by date, bucketed by sku_id; forecasts partitioned by run_date
(c) ModelProphet: weekly and yearly seasonality, holidays (Eid, Puja, Pohela Boishakh), automatic changepoints, tolerates gaps. ARIMA needs hand tuning per series; LSTM needs much data, GPUs and is a black box
(d) Parallel fitdaily.groupBy("sku_id").applyInPandas(fit, schema); each group goes to one task, Prophet fits inside the Pandas UDF
(e) ServeWrite Parquet to Hive/S3; load latest run into a serving table; dashboard (Superset/Grafana) shows yhat with bands and reorder alerts

Numbers: 8 h = 480 min sequential; 12 min on 20 executors; speedup = 480 / 12 = 40×; 5.76 s per model; 250 models per executor. One at a time that is 250 × 5.76 = 1,440 s = 24 min, so the slide's 12 min implies about 2 models at once per executor (40 slots).

Bottleneck: model fitting (Prophet via Stan, the 8-hour step). Skewed SKUs with long histories finish last; cap history and add cores.

pool.q: Kwak et al. found Twitter's average shortest path is 4.12 hops over 41.7M users. If a misinformation tweet is retweeted by a high-PageRank account, estimate how many users it reaches within 3 hops assuming an average out-degree of 45. What graph property makes this estimate an overestimate? [CLO4 — Apply]
pool.a:
Estimate: 45 + 45² + 45³ = 45 + 2,025 + 91,125 = 93,195 users (0.22% of 41.7M).

For an overestimate: clustering. Followers overlap, so the tree counts the same people again; most viewers also do not retweet.

Against: a high-PageRank account may have over a million followers, so hop 1 alone can beat 45.

pool.q: A Prophet model for weekly hospital admissions has strong annual and weekly seasonality but misses a sudden COVID-19 wave onset. Identify which Prophet component should detect this changepoint and explain what prior hyperparameter controls the model's sensitivity to new changepoints. [CLO4 — Analyse]
pool.a:
Component: the trend g(t). A wave is a structural break, not a repeating cycle or a listed holiday.

Hyperparameter: changepoint_prior_scale, the scale of the sparse prior on the slope changes δ. Default 0.05 keeps the trend stiff and smooths over the wave; raising it (e.g. 0.5) lets the trend bend.

Against raising it: the trend then chases noise and the forecast band widens, so tune on held-out weeks.

• Sources: ED visits (FHIR) as main signal, NS1 lab results, dengue tweets as leading signal, rainfall.

pool.q: Live Exercise — Prophet Flu Forecasting in Python. Task (25 minutes, pairs): Fit a Prophet model to synthetic weekly flu incidence data and produce a 12-week forecast. Install: pip install prophet matplotlib pandas
pool.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from prophet import Prophet
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.date_range("2021-01-04",
                      periods=156, freq="W")
# Annual flu seasonality + noise
ili = (5 + 3*np.sin(
          2*np.pi*np.arange(156)/52
          - np.pi/2)
       + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 156)).clip(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({"ds": dates, "y": ili})

# Optional: add Eid holiday
holidays = pd.DataFrame({
   "holiday": "Eid",
   "ds":       pd.to_datetime([
                 "2021-05-13","2022-05-03",
                 "2023-04-22"]),
   "lower_window": 0,
   "upper_window": 3,
})

m = Prophet(
    yearly_seasonality=True,
    weekly_seasonality=False,
    changepoint_prior_scale=0.05,
    holidays=holidays)
m.fit(df)
future = m.make_future_dataframe(
    periods=12, freq="W")
forecast = m.predict(future)
m.plot(forecast)
m.plot_components(forecast)
plt.show()
pool.a:
Run the skeleton, then refit with the changes below.

m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True,
            weekly_seasonality=False,
            changepoint_prior_scale=0.05,   # try 0.5
            holidays=holidays,
            interval_width=0.95)            # 95% band
m.fit(df)
fc = m.predict(m.make_future_dataframe(periods=12, freq="W"))
m.plot(fc); m.plot_components(fc)

Expected: dates run 2021-01-10 to 2023-12-31 (weeks end Sunday); the forecast covers 2024-01-07 to 2024-03-24 and rises from the yearly low (true curve 2.0) towards about 4.3.

pool.q: Generate 3 years of synthetic weekly ILI data with annual seasonality + noise.
pool.a: The skeleton does it: 156 weekly dates (156 / 52 = 3 years), a sine with period 52 weeks running from 2 to 8 around a mean of 5, plus noise with SD 0.5. Columns must be named ds and y.

pool.q: Fit Prophet with yearly and weekly seasonality.
pool.a: yearly_seasonality=True fits the annual Fourier wave (P = 365.25). Keep weekly_seasonality=False: with one point per week, always a Sunday, there is no within-week pattern to learn.

pool.q: Plot the forecast with 95% uncertainty intervals.
pool.a: Pass interval_width=0.95 (default is 80%), then m.plot(forecast). Expected: data dots, the yhat line and a band from yhat_lower to yhat_upper that widens into the future.

pool.q: Add a holiday for “Eid” (spike in healthcare visits) and observe the effect.
pool.a: Expected effect is near zero: the synthetic data has no Eid spike, and the 2022 window (05-03 to 05-06) contains no Sunday, so it matches no point. Add +3 to the Eid weeks and the components plot shows an Eid bar near +3.

pool.q: Change changepoint_prior_scale from 0.05 to 0.5 and compare trend flexibility.
pool.a: At 0.05 the trend stays nearly flat around 5 (the true trend). At 0.5 it wiggles, absorbs noise and part of the seasonal wave, and the future band widens. Higher reacts faster to real breaks but overfits stable data.

b.q:
A hospital group forecasts weekly admissions for 400 wards with Prophet.
i) Write the Prophet model and name each term. (2)
ii) In an Eid week, g = 80, s = +6, h = +12, ε = 0. Forecast? (1)
iii) Each ward's model takes 2 s; Spark fits 20 at a time. Sequential time, parallel time? (1)
iv) The model missed a sudden COVID wave. Which term should catch it, and which hyperparameter controls that? (2)
b.a: i) y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t): trend, seasonality, holidays, noise. ii) 80 + 6 + 12 + 0 = 98. iii) 400 × 2 = 800 s; 800 / 20 = 40 s (20×). iv) Trend g(t) via changepoints; changepoint_prior_scale (raise from 0.05 to bend faster).

or_a.q:
DGHS wants one sepsis model from 30 hospitals and a public dashboard of cases by upazila.
i) How can it train without pooling records? (1)
ii) How can it stop small counts revealing a patient? (1)
iii) Which US law requires removing 18 identifiers? (1)
iv) A linked genomics study has 5,000 patients at 200 GB each. Storage in PB? (1)
or_a.a: i) Federated learning. ii) Differential privacy. iii) HIPAA. iv) 5,000 × 200 = 1,000,000 GB = 1 PB.

or_b.q:
A researcher studies a misinformation cascade on X.
i) Give the steps of Louvain for finding the groups that spread it. (2)
ii) Average out-degree is 40. Upper bound on users reached in 2 hops? (1)
iii) Why is that an overestimate? (1)
iv) Kwak et al. found 22.1% reciprocity. What does that say about Twitter compared with Facebook? (2)
or_b.a: i) Each node alone; move nodes to the neighbour community with the biggest modularity gain; collapse to super-nodes; repeat until no gain. ii) 40 + 1,600 = 1,640. iii) Followers overlap (clustering), so people are counted twice, and not everyone reshares. iv) Most follows are one-way, so Twitter is a directed news medium; Facebook friendship is mutual (≈100%), a social network.
